episode_title: Halfway From Coal, Halfway to Diamond

stories.summary: Amit was living in a village in a district he won't name and asked Ajay where to get a haircut. Ajay sent him to the village barber shop. There was no electricity and Amit could hardly see the mirror, and before he knew it the sides of his head were gone. Ajay raised the haircut the moment Amit promised the show would cover 'the profane' as well as the profound.
stories.insight: A self-deprecating opener that sets the show's tone: two people known for policy and economics agreeing to be playful as well as serious.
stories.quote: Haircut doesn't really suit my age, but you know, hey, I'm a city slicker, I've come to a village. Let me just get the village haircut.

stories.topic: The Snake That Forgot to Hide Its Tail
stories.summary: Amit had walk-run almost 7 km on Ajay's track and was exhausted, sure he couldn't go any faster. While he was cooling down, a snake shot across the path into the bushes and waited there with its tail still lying on the path. He turned and sprinted. His Garmin logged about 25 km/h, which Ajay told him is about the top speed a human can reach.
stories.insight: Fear found reserves that the tired mind had written off. It also previews Ajay's later point that when an event ambushes us, we act from deep instinct and only afterwards get to ask whether that instinct was right.
stories.quote: I thought this is a stupid snake, it thinks I can't see it, but the tail is there. And then I was like, play it safe, boy, and I turned around and I sprinted madly.

stories.topic: India's Big Four Venomous Snakes Are Not Alike
stories.summary: Ajay went through the four venomous snakes behind most bad encounters in India. Cobras live around human settlements and have reached a working coexistence with people: they flash their hoods, people run, and many apparent strikes are made with the mouth closed. Kraits are quiet and calm. The trouble comes when one seeks a sleeping person's warmth and gets crushed, and as Amit adds, the bite is painless, so the victim simply dies in their sleep. The tiny saw-scaled viper puts on a scary display that usually works, except on young men who try to pick it up by the tail. Only the Russell's viper strikes with no reasonable provocation.
stories.insight: Our fear is poorly matched to the real danger. The snakes people dread most have adapted to living alongside humans. Before you fear a whole category, look at how its members actually behave.
stories.quote: So the cobras are much less dangerous than is widely considered.

stories.summary: By a lakeside in Udaipur, Ajay once told Amit that seagulls are bastards. They are effectively birds of prey: they kill and eat pigeons, tear chunks of flesh from the backs of baby whales near the surface, and have been reported gouging out the eyes of seals. Amit added that seagulls go for the eyes first, and that they practise kleptoparasitism, stealing food from others, 'like stealing from a thief'. That made him think of the License Raj state taxing the rent-seekers and cronies it had created.
stories.insight: We decide what an animal is like from how it looks, which is an anthropocentric mistake, and the gap between image and behaviour unsettles us. The conversation then turns to why we don't judge animals morally but do judge humans.
stories.quote: So we think of a seagull, it should be some nice vegetarian bird. Okay, it's not that.

stories.summary: At a book event, Shrayana Bhattacharya, author of Desperately Seeking Shah Rukh, told Amit he was an 'anti-uncle'. She meant that he is willing to change his mind, listens to arguments from the other side, stays open to ideas and will engage with anyone. The 'uncle' is the opposite: closed, settled in a worldview and insistent on it.
stories.insight: What makes someone an 'uncle' is mental rigidity, not age. That sets up the episode's longer discussion of conformism.
stories.quote: she paid me what I think is one of the finest compliments I've ever received, where she said, Amit, you are an anti-uncle.

stories.summary: Galileo was forced to recant his observation that the earth goes around the sun and to say he had been wrong. Amit tells how he came out afterwards, looked up at the sky, stamped the ground and said 'Eppur si muove': still it turns. In Paul Graham's essay, this is the call of the aggressively independent-minded.
stories.insight: Power can force people to say they agree, but it cannot change what is true.
stories.quote: verbally fall in line with the conventional-minded, but that doesn't change the reality.

stories.topic: Old Classmates Resurface to Call Him an Asshole
stories.summary: Amit wrote a deliberately provocative column arguing that it is immoral to have children. The backlash was so strong that people he had not heard from since school, 35 years earlier, found him on Facebook just to call him an asshole.
stories.insight: A funny but telling example of what it costs to argue against received wisdom in public. It sets up Ajay's point about the market failure in criticism.
stories.quote: since thirty-five years ago in school got in touch with me on Facebook to tell me I was an asshole.

stories.topic: Hussain Haidry's Loneliness in a Mob
stories.summary: The poet Hussain Haidry, a guest on The Seen and the Unseen, told Amit that when right-wing accounts mobbed him, what hurt was how alone he felt: nobody called to say they were with him or to ask how he was. Amit has been targeted by both right-wing and woke mobs and recognises the feeling. Even with many well-wishers, nobody grasps what it is like when a thousand people are abusing you within an hour.
stories.insight: Being mobbed is isolating, and that isolation is how mobs chill speech. Over time people stop saying what they think, until they no longer even think it.
stories.quote: when he was mobbed by the right wing guys, he said he felt so alone.

stories.summary: Billy Joel's 'Piano Man' nearly vanished, and Joel was not going to make more music. One man loved the song so much that he went from radio station to radio station asking them to play it. He finally struck a deal with someone at a big station, almost a bribe, to get it on air. The song became a hit and Joel went on to make many more albums. Amit adds that Bach only became a big name decades after he died.
stories.insight: Talent alone does not decide which art survives; luck and the people who champion it matter a great deal. That raises the question of how many masterpieces disappear because nobody pushed for them.
stories.quote: So there's so much luck involved as well.

recommendations.item: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time
recommendations.creator: Mark Haddon
recommendations.context: Amit's book of the week, after a short case for why reading matters. A 15-year-old boy investigates who killed his neighbour's dog, and the story is told in his voice.
recommendations.reason: It shows what fiction can do: let you live inside a very different mind. Amit read out Haddon's own description: 'it's a novel about difference, about being an outsider, about seeing the world in a surprising and revealing way. It's as much a novel about us as it is about Christopher.'

recommendations.item: Songs of Surrender
recommendations.creator: U2
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation of the week, released about two months before the episode. U2 rework 40 songs, mostly old with a few new.
recommendations.reason: U2 rethink songs they wrote as kids from a more grown-up place, changing arrangements and editing lyrics. It is not a set formula like MTV Unplugged. Ajay also likes the thought that some young listeners will start here and only later go back to The Joshua Tree and The Unforgettable Fire.

recommendations.item: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Prompted by the 'anti-uncle' compliment, Amit called it one of the finest essays he has read in recent years and read out the passage on the four 'calls'.
recommendations.reason: It gives a clear map of conventional versus independent thinkers, each either passive or aggressive. It also explains why the aggressively conventional-minded are the loudest on social media and the ones who hold back progress.

recommendations.item: Private Truths, Public Lies
recommendations.creator: Timur Kuran
recommendations.context: Ajay brought up Kuran's idea of preference falsification. Amit said he keeps citing this book, and mentioned that Ajay had told him the night before that Kuran was once his teacher.
recommendations.reason: It explains preference falsification and preference cascades. Amit uses them to explain the collapse of Soviet communism, the Modi wave and the open bigotry that social media unlocked.

recommendations.item: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
recommendations.creator: Thomas Nagel
recommendations.context: An early-seventies philosophy essay Amit raised while explaining why fiction matters.
recommendations.reason: Nagel argues that we can describe how a bat experiences the world through echolocation but can never imagine it. Amit uses this as a contrast: through stories we do manage to imagine other people's lives.

recommendations.item: The Tell-Tale Brain
recommendations.creator: VS Ramachandran
recommendations.context: Amit recalled Ramachandran telling him all about mirror neurons at a TED event, before he wrote the book that covers them at length.
recommendations.reason: It explains the science behind empathy: mirror neurons copy the experiences of others when we hear about them. That is part of why reading other people's lives works on us.

recommendations.item: Lessons from an Ankhon Dekhi Prime Minister
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on the importance of reading, linked while he talked about books.
recommendations.reason: It develops his argument that personal experience gives us only a few dots, slowly, while books let us collect many dots fast and connect them into an understanding of the world.

recommendations.item: Population Is Not a Problem, but Our Greatest Strength
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The first of three columns Amit cited that drew furious responses from the aggressively conventional-minded.
recommendations.reason: It challenges the school lesson that population is India's biggest problem. People are brains, not stomachs, and the problems blamed on population are really failures of governance.

recommendations.item: India's Problem Is Poverty, Not Inequality
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The second provocative column Amit cited.
recommendations.reason: It separates two problems that people routinely confuse and that need opposite solutions. It is built around the question of whether you would rather be poor in the USA or in Bangladesh.

recommendations.item: It Is Immoral to Have Children. Here's Why
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The third column, the one that brought old school acquaintances out to abuse him.
recommendations.reason: It is a deliberately provocative argument. We agree not to do things to people without consent, not to cause pain and not to kill, yet a child is born without consent, will feel pain and will die. Amit says the argument has to be tackled, while admitting he might do things he thinks are immoral.

recommendations.item: Kashi Ka Assi
recommendations.creator: Kashinath Singh
recommendations.context: Amit took his personal approach to social media trolls, 'harmonia', from a famous phrase in this novel.
recommendations.reason: It gives him a stance: don't bother, block every toxic or rude account, and use the platform instead to build a feed of the finest minds in the world.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay cited it during the discussion of the cost of being a public critic.
recommendations.reason: In it, Kelkar and Shah argue that criticism suffers from a market failure: critics create benefits for everyone but bear the cost themselves. Ajay suggests social media has made that failure bigger.

recommendations.item: Desperately Seeking Shah Rukh
recommendations.creator: Shrayana Bhattacharya
recommendations.context: Amit mentioned it while introducing Shrayana, who called him an 'anti-uncle' at a book event they did together.
recommendations.reason: Amit introduced it as Shrayana's book, and the 'anti-uncle' compliment came from her. The book is also the subject of his 'great' Seen and the Unseen episode with her.

recommendations.item: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shrayana Bhattacharya
recommendations.context: Mentioned when Amit introduced Shrayana Bhattacharya.
recommendations.reason: Amit called it a great episode. It is the longer conversation with the person who gave him the 'anti-uncle' label.

recommendations.item: Hussain Haidry, Hindustani Musalmaan (Episode 275 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Hussain Haidry
recommendations.context: Linked when Amit told how Hussain felt alone while being mobbed by the right wing.
recommendations.reason: It is a fuller conversation with the poet whose experience shows what online mobs do to the people they target.

recommendations.item: In a Silent Way (Episode 316 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Gaurav Chintamani
recommendations.context: Mentioned in the discussion of artists getting frozen into their old hits.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great episode in which the musician talks about how a big hit can become a curse: you keep changing, but audiences keep shouting a three-minute song from twenty years ago at you.

recommendations.item: Eric Weinstein Won't Toe the Line (Episode 330 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Eric Weinstein
recommendations.context: Amit had put his question about the missing masterpieces to Eric in this episode, and Eric strongly disagreed.
recommendations.reason: It is the longer version of the debate this episode ends on: with far more potential artists alive than ever before, why don't we see more great art?

recommendations.item: Is Old Music Killing New Music?
recommendations.creator: Ted Gioia
recommendations.context: Amit thought he only listened to old comfort music because he was getting older, and then read this piece.
recommendations.reason: Gioia's data shows old music is outselling new music by a mile. Amit's own habits turned out to be part of a structural shift in the industry, not just ageing.

recommendations.item: The Time a Stiff Caught Fire
recommendations.creator: Keith Yates
recommendations.context: Amit called it a 'very moving story' and linked it in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It tells the full story of the fan who got 'Piano Man' onto the radio and saved Billy Joel's career, which shows how much luck decides what we later call great art.

recommendations.item: Beat a Drum
recommendations.creator: R.E.M.
recommendations.context: Ajay said his phrase 'halfway from coal, halfway to diamond', which became the episode's title, is taken from an R.E.M. song.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of the episode's central image of people as unfinished works in progress.

recommendations.item: YouTube Music (discovery playlists)
recommendations.context: Ajay's reply when Amit asked whether he still discovers new music.
recommendations.reason: You just ask it for a playlist without having to think, and it brings you new things. Ajay has been astonished by how much newer music he has found and liked this way.

recommendations.item: The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Discussed at the start of the episode and again in the reading segment.
recommendations.reason: Ajay describes it as having become oral history, with three-to-eight-hour deep dives into one person at a time. Its show notes list every book mentioned, and that list has become a meme, 'the Seen and the Unseen bookshelf'.

core_ideas.concept: Hardware vs Software: Culture Is Our Operating System
core_ideas.explanation: A newborn king cobra is fully a king cobra at birth: its behaviour is hard-coded and stays the same for life. Higher animals add culture, meaning learned behaviours, beliefs and heuristics, and in humans this becomes a whole operating system. Only humans can examine that operating system and rewrite it. That is why we don't morally judge a cobra but do ask questions about our own code. In Ajay's words, this plasticity is what makes us human.
core_ideas.quote: So culture, that plasticity is what makes us human.

core_ideas.concept: Character Is Contingent, but Act as if Free Will Exists
core_ideas.explanation: Animals do brutal things and we don't judge them. Humans are animals too, and much of what we call reasoning is rationalisation of where our instincts already took us. We are shaped by genes and circumstances; Amit quotes Steven Pinker: 'Nature gives us knobs, nurture turns them'. That could argue for never judging anyone. But a society needs a code that punishes the bad and rewards the good, so Amit concludes we should keep holding people responsible anyway.
core_ideas.quote: I think that even if there is no free will for civilization to progress, we must behave as if there is.

core_ideas.concept: Judge the Algorithm, Not the Outcome
core_ideas.explanation: We are all works in progress, 'halfway from coal, halfway to diamond'. Because the world is probabilistic, a good decision can turn out badly. So instead of grading outcomes, look at the process that produced the decision. When an event ambushes us we react on instinct; growth means reflecting afterwards on whether that instinct was right. Neither 'we are fully determined' nor 'we are fully free' is true. What counts is to keep trying.
core_ideas.quote: So I always like to say don't judge a decision by its outcome because the world is probabilistic.

core_ideas.concept: Uncles, Anti-Uncles and the Four Quadrants of Conformism
core_ideas.explanation: Paul Graham sorts people into conventional-minded and independent-minded, each either passive or aggressive, and gives each type a 'call'. Aggressively conventional: 'Crush outgroup!' Passively conventional: 'What will the neighbours think?' Passively independent: 'To each his own.' Aggressively independent: 'Eppur si muove.' Amit's point is that the aggressively conventional-minded, whatever their tribe (right-wing, woke or otherwise), make the most noise online and get in the way of progress. They repeat memorised slogans loudly and shut down dialogue. His personal fix is to notice that his own first reaction to a radical idea is 'no', and to push back on it, because every idea that changes the world starts out as a radical idea.
core_ideas.quote: the loudest noise on Twitter and social media is actually made by the aggressively conventional-minded. These are not people saying anything new.

core_ideas.explanation: Indians are taught in school that population is the country's biggest problem. Amit argues the opposite. Human history is a long migration from villages to cities, the places where population density is highest, because more people means more minds working together. The problems blamed on population are failures of governance. And people who complain about population never count themselves in it.
core_ideas.quote: And everyone who says population is a problem will never include themselves as part of the population.

core_ideas.explanation: Ask whether you would rather be poor in the USA or in Bangladesh. Everyone picks the USA, even though it has more inequality as measured by the Gini coefficient. After liberalisation, India lifted more than 400 million people out of poverty while inequality rose. The belief that the rich getting richer means the poor getting poorer comes from zero-sum thinking. Poverty and inequality are different problems with opposite solutions, and India's problem is poverty.
core_ideas.quote: in which of these two countries would you rather be poor, the USA or Bangladesh?

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay looks at conformists as an economist would, as people optimising. Tribal networks give warmth, connection and a route to power, and loudly enforcing the norms is the ticket in. Many 'uncles' are not true believers; they are using an ideology to get ahead, and they will change sides overnight when it pays. That makes Ajay fairly kind towards them. Amit accepts this as an explanation but not as a justification, because social media makes the damage they do much bigger.
core_ideas.quote: People are not wood, people are not stones, people are optimizers.

core_ideas.explanation: Timur Kuran's idea: three months before communism collapsed, everyone in East Germany and the USSR publicly professed the official beliefs and almost nobody privately held them. Some went along quietly; others aggressively policed anyone who broke the rules. A preference cascade is what happens once people realise others feel the same way they do: the public pretence collapses quickly. Amit argues the same thing happened in reverse with social media in India. Bigots who had kept quiet in polite society saw that many others shared their views, so they stopped hiding, and politicians no longer needed dog whistles. He sees the same dynamic in Trump's rise.
core_ideas.quote: And in their heart, nobody had those beliefs. But it was wise and efficient to say that as a way to get along, as a way to gain power.

core_ideas.explanation: Critics make progress possible for everyone, but they personally absorb the attacks. In economists' terms, they create a positive externality and pay a high private cost, so society gets less criticism than it needs. Ajay suspects social media has made this failure bigger than it was in earlier times. Amit adds the chilling effect: mob behaviour makes people stop saying what they feel, until eventually they stop feeling it.
core_ideas.quote: Because the critic personally takes the brunt of all the attacks that come by. But actually all the progress of the world is only made possible by the critics.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay has stayed off social media entirely, while Amit uses it heavily. Ajay separates two questions: what should I personally do, and how is this phenomenon changing the world? A thinker has to take the second seriously whatever their answer to the first. Amit's personal answer is curation: block every toxic account and build a feed of the best minds thinking aloud, which he says would have seemed like magic in 1985. As a public intellectual, though, he accepts that unpopular positions cost him in career and mental health.
core_ideas.quote: coldly understanding how this phenomenon is acting upon the world.

core_ideas.explanation: We make sense of the world by connecting dots. Personal experience supplies few dots and takes years to do it, while books supply many dots quickly. Fiction lets you live other people's lives, and mirror neurons mean we are wired to feel what others feel. Ajay extends this to non-fiction: a great book of ideas holds the work of one person's whole life, so reading it is like living an extra life. That is the opposite of the practitioner 'living the same day over and over'. Amit also rejects the claim that attention spans are dying, saying people still crave depth.
core_ideas.quote: books offer you not an escape from life but an embrace of it.

core_ideas.explanation: The market makes artists into one fixed version of themselves: U2 is expected to sound like The Joshua Tree forever, and Radiohead are sick of playing 'Creep', an angsty song from their youth. Part of the cause was format, the three-minute single, the forty-minute album and the album-tour-album cycle. Today bands can change songs day to day on YouTube and Discord. Ajay applies the same idea to people: no man crosses the same river twice, and the Gandhi of 1919 was very different from the Gandhi of 1939. Holding someone to what they said at one moment is unfair to their journey.
core_ideas.quote: you're ossified into that one three-minute package thing that you did twenty years ago.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's half-joking theory: macroeconomists tamed the business cycle, and Robert Lucas said of the 2008 crisis response, 'we won'. But misery and hardship fuel art, so great music may now come from the troubled places of the world. Amit replies that we are lucky to have escaped such times, and that many people in India still live through extreme hardship. Ajay points to Tagore, who was personally privileged but connected to a difficult era, and concludes that good art may be counter-cyclical.
core_ideas.quote: good times are the worst thing that you can supply as fuel for the young people who would then go on to build the art.

core_ideas.explanation: Ted Gioia's data shows old music outselling new. One explanation, backed by some research, is that our musical taste is formed roughly between ages 16 and 26 and then fixed for life. Ajay points out that this cannot be the whole story. Few people who were young in the 70s are still listening, yet Dark Side of the Moon remains one of the most successful albums of all time. Amit adds that fragmentation is also a gain: musicians no longer depend on labels, and listeners can find very personal niches.
core_ideas.quote: And yet Dark Side of the Moon remains one of the most successful albums of all time.

core_ideas.concept: Where Are the Masterpieces? (In Art and Science)
core_ideas.explanation: Far more people alive today have the means to make art than ever before; Ajay's example is how many more Indians can now buy a sitar and hire a teacher. Statistically, more geniuses should appear. Amit offers possible reasons: we overrate past work, the early works opened doors that only needed opening once, or today's masterpieces get lost in a fragmented market. Ajay sees the same puzzle in science. Rutherford discovered the nucleus with a simple apparatus he could hold in his hands, and Einstein wrote four world-changing papers in one year. Funding is now up a millionfold, yet fundamental breakthroughs seem slower.
core_ideas.quote: So I think there is a concern that something about the machine, something about the modern world, is interfering with the great leaps.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit says he wants the show to cover 'not just about the profound, but also the profane'. Ajay's immediate reply: 'How did you get that interesting haircut?'

Amit compares the snake with its tail sticking out to a scene in an Amitabh Bachchan–Shashi Kapoor film where the two are bathing naked, a woman opens the door, and they cover the wrong thing: 'this is a stupid snake, it thinks I can't see it, but the tail is there.'
Ajay on Amit's 25 km/h sprint: he'll be a well-adjusted villager when 'the tail of a snake will no longer excite peaks of physical performance.'

Amit says seagulls are not just bastards but 'lazy bastards', because they steal food from others, 'like stealing from a thief'. He compares this to the License Raj state taxing the rent-seekers and cronies it had created.
Amit on who gets to be an 'uncle': only men can be uncles, while 'women can be Karens, I guess.'
Paul Graham's line, read by Amit, on the aggressively conventional-minded whose call is 'Crush outgroup!': 'It's rather alarming to see an exclamation point after a variable.'
Amit on population alarmists: they never count themselves as part of the population, their message is just 'you stop having babies.'

Amit says Amazon's algorithm shows the Seen and the Unseen bookshelf effect: open the page of one book he recommended and Amazon suggests five more with no connection to each other, except that he recommended all of them.

Amit on the old music-industry cycle, in Hinglish: release an album, tour for two years, release another album, and then you become an old band that only comes to India to perform hits from forty years ago.
Ajay on how far macroeconomics has come: 'The Great Depression gave us Adolf Hitler. The 2008 crisis only gave us Donald Trump. Okay, so we've clearly come a long way.'

Ajay complains that all the money poured into science has given us 'trivial things like food delivery apps and what I consider a relatively trivial innovation, the LLMs'. Amit, closing the show, says we should uninstall the food apps from our phones 'and cook our own food.'
Amit, apologising for being new to video: 'I like to keep joking that I have a face for audio, which clearly you can see is true.'
'Halfway from coal, halfway to diamond', Ajay's image of people as works in progress and the episode's title, is taken from the R.E.M. song 'Beat a Drum'.
Steven Pinker, quoted by Amit: 'Nature gives us knobs, nurture turns them.'
Galileo's 'Eppur si muove' ('and still it turns'), which Paul Graham uses as the call of the aggressively independent-minded.

Glenn Reynolds, the blogger known as Instapundit, whom Amit cites as arguing that Trump's rise came from letting xenophobia into the open. If Trump could say Mexicans are rapists, people with similar prejudices could embrace him.
Steve Van Zandt's point, as Amit recalls it, that rock and roll began when Dylan went electric and ended when Kurt Cobain died.
Robert Lucas, cited by Ajay, saying 'we won' about the response to the 2008 crisis, as evidence that macroeconomists have tamed the business cycle.
'No man can cross the same river twice. He's not the same and the river is not the same.' Ajay uses it to argue that ideas and people should not be frozen at one moment.

Rutherford's famous photo holding the simple apparatus with which he fired alpha particles at gold foil and found the nucleus, and Einstein's four world-changing papers in a single year. Ajay offers both as examples of how much science once got from so little.
Radiohead being sick of performing 'Creep', a breakaway hit written when they were 'immature young men', which Amit cites as an artist trapped by an old song.
The MAMI film festival, which Amit says was his yearly vacation for many years until COVID.
